::: {.objectives}
**Goals.** Build an `sf` object from a CSV; reproject it; measure distances
correctly (and incorrectly, so you can see the difference); read a real raster
and sample it at your fixes; make an undistorted map.

**Time:** ~50 minutes. **Packages:** `sf`, `terra`, `dplyr`.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(sf)
library(terra)
library(dplyr)
```
:::


## Task 1 — From data frame to `sf`


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
buffalo <- read.csv("data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz") |>
  transmute(
    id = individual.local.identifier,
    t  = as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"),
    lon = location.long,
    lat = location.lat
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(lon), !is.na(lat)) |>
  distinct(id, t, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  arrange(id, t)

nrow(buffalo)
#> [1] 24663

buf_sf <- st_as_sf(buffalo, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE)
buf_sf
#> Simple feature collection with 24663 features and 4 fields
#> Geometry type: POINT
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: 31.58639 ymin: -25.16421 xmax: 32.35671 ymax: -23.99802
#> Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84
#> First 10 features:
#>       id                   t      lon       lat                   geometry
#> 1  Cilla 2005-07-14 04:35:00 31.80449 -25.06147 POINT (31.80449 -25.06147)
#> 2  Cilla 2005-07-14 05:35:00 31.88776 -24.96738 POINT (31.88776 -24.96738)
#> 3  Cilla 2005-07-14 07:35:00 31.85942 -24.94288 POINT (31.85942 -24.94288)
#> 4  Cilla 2005-07-14 08:34:00 31.85512 -24.94914 POINT (31.85512 -24.94914)
#> 5  Cilla 2005-07-14 09:35:00 31.85694 -24.95424 POINT (31.85694 -24.95424)
#> 6  Cilla 2005-07-14 10:35:00 31.85977 -24.94735 POINT (31.85977 -24.94735)
#> 7  Cilla 2005-07-14 11:34:00 31.84466 -24.93435 POINT (31.84466 -24.93435)
#> 8  Cilla 2005-07-14 12:35:00 31.84410 -24.93400    POINT (31.8441 -24.934)
#> 9  Cilla 2005-07-14 13:34:00 31.84463 -24.93442 POINT (31.84463 -24.93442)
#> 10 Cilla 2005-07-14 14:35:00 31.85700 -24.93371   POINT (31.857 -24.93371)
```
:::


::: {.callout-tip}
`remove = FALSE` keeps the original `lon`/`lat` columns. Handy — you often
want the plain numbers alongside the geometry.
:::

### Your turn

**1a.** What does `st_crs(buf_sf)` report? Find the EPSG code and the units.
**1b.** What is the bounding box?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
st_crs(buf_sf)$epsg
#> [1] 4326
st_crs(buf_sf)$units_gdal
#> [1] "degree"
st_is_longlat(buf_sf)
#> [1] TRUE

st_bbox(buf_sf)
#>      xmin      ymin      xmax      ymax 
#>  31.58639 -25.16421  32.35671 -23.99802
```
:::


Degrees, EPSG:4326, and `st_is_longlat()` is `TRUE` — the flag that should
make you stop before computing any distance or area.
:::

## Task 2 — Reproject, and watch the numbers change

Kruger sits in UTM zone 36S, EPSG:32736.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
buf_utm <- st_transform(buf_sf, 32736)

# Same animal, same fix, different numbers
st_coordinates(buf_sf)[1, ]
#>         X         Y 
#>  31.80449 -25.06147
st_coordinates(buf_utm)[1, ]
#>         X         Y 
#>  379415.9 7227712.7
```
:::


::: {.callout-important}
## Which zone?

`zone = floor((longitude + 180) / 6) + 1`. Kruger is at ~31.8°E, so
`floor(211.8 / 6) + 1 = 36`. Southern hemisphere → EPSG `327` + zone = **32736**.
Northern would be `326` + zone.
:::

### Your turn

**2a.** Confirm the round trip: transform back to 4326 and compare to the original.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
back <- st_transform(buf_utm, 4326)
max(abs(st_coordinates(back) - st_coordinates(buf_sf)))
#> [1] 1.776357e-14
```
:::


Agreement to ~1e-9 degrees — about 0.1 mm. Reprojection is lossless up to
floating-point precision; it is not a source of error you need to worry about.
:::

## Task 3 — Three ways to measure one distance

Take the first two fixes of buffalo "Queen" and measure the step three ways.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
queen <- buf_sf |> filter(id == "Queen") |> slice(1:2)

# (1) WRONG — Euclidean on degrees, pretending they are metres
xy <- st_coordinates(queen)
wrong <- sqrt(diff(xy[, 1])^2 + diff(xy[, 2])^2)
wrong
#> [1] 0.002835514

# (2) Geodesic on the ellipsoid — sf does this automatically for 4326
geodesic <- st_distance(queen[1, ], queen[2, ])
geodesic
#> Units: [m]
#>          [,1]
#> [1,] 301.4658

# (3) Euclidean in projected metres
queen_utm <- st_transform(queen, 32736)
projected <- st_distance(queen_utm[1, ], queen_utm[2, ])
projected
#> Units: [m]
#>          [,1]
#> [1,] 300.9957
```
:::


### Your turn

**3a.** Explain the three numbers.
**3b.** How big is the disagreement between (2) and (3), in relative terms?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
c(wrong_degrees = as.numeric(wrong),
  geodesic_m    = as.numeric(geodesic),
  projected_m   = as.numeric(projected))
#> wrong_degrees    geodesic_m   projected_m 
#>  2.835514e-03  3.014658e+02  3.009957e+02

# Relative difference between the two *correct* methods
abs(as.numeric(geodesic) - as.numeric(projected)) / as.numeric(geodesic)
#> [1] 0.001559558
```
:::


Number (1) is in **degrees** and is not a distance at all — it is a
dimensionless mix of two different angular units. It is small not because the
animal barely moved, but because degrees are big.

Numbers (2) and (3) are both in metres and agree to a small fraction of a
percent. That is UTM doing its job: inside one zone, distortion is under 0.1%.

**Practical rule.** For distances, either is fine inside a zone. But for
kernel density, step-length distributions, buffers and anything involving
*area*, project first — those methods assume a plane.
:::

## Task 4 — Scale up: all steps for all animals


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
step_lengths <- buf_utm |>
  group_by(id) |>
  arrange(t, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    sl = as.numeric(st_distance(geometry, lag(geometry), by_element = TRUE)),
    dt = as.numeric(difftime(t, lag(t), units = "hours"))
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(!is.na(sl))

summary(step_lengths$sl)
#>     Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. 
#>     0.00    28.54   153.92   330.34   399.99 63102.52
```
:::


### Your turn

**4a.** What is the median step length per individual?
**4b.** Plot the distribution of step lengths. Why the long tail?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
step_lengths |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(n = n(), median_sl = median(sl), max_sl = max(sl), .groups = "drop")
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   id         n median_sl max_sl
#>   <chr>  <int>     <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 Cilla   3527      149. 13386.
#> 2 Gabs    3669      107.  6112.
#> 3 Mvubu   2571      127.  6114.
#> 4 Pepper  4570      181. 21244.
#> 5 Queen   4544      171. 16082.
#> 6 Toni    5776      174. 63103.
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(step_lengths$sl, breaks = 60, col = "#1f6f78", border = "white",
     main = "Step lengths", xlab = "metres")
hist(log10(step_lengths$sl + 1), breaks = 60, col = "#1f6f78", border = "white",
     main = "log10(step length + 1)", xlab = "log10 metres")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```
:::


Two things produce the tail. First, genuine long movements. Second — and this
is the important one — **steps separated by long time gaps**. A "step" across
a 12-hour gap is not comparable to a step across one hour.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(step_lengths$dt, step_lengths$sl, pch = 16, cex = 0.2,
     col = adjustcolor("#1f6f78", 0.3), log = "y",
     xlab = "Time gap (hours)", ylab = "Step length (m), log scale")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-align='center' width=576}
:::
:::


Step length is meaningless without its time interval. This is why Class 3
**resamples** tracks to a regular interval before computing anything.
:::

## Task 5 — A real raster

We use SRTM-derived elevation for the Kruger area, already cropped for you.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
elev <- rast("data/kruger_elevation.tif")
elev
#> class       : SpatRaster
#> size        : 168, 132, 1  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
#> resolution  : 0.008333333, 0.008333333  (x, y)
#> extent      : 31.4, 32.5, -25.3, -23.9  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
#> coord. ref. : lon/lat WGS 84 (EPSG:4326)
#> source      : kruger_elevation.tif
#> name        : elevation
#> min value   :       117
#> max value   :       572
```
:::


### Your turn

**5a.** What is the resolution, in degrees and roughly in metres?
**5b.** Extract elevation at every buffalo fix. What is the range?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
res(elev)                       # degrees
#> [1] 0.008333333 0.008333333
res(elev)[2] * 111320           # metres, north-south
#> [1] 927.6667
res(elev)[1] * 111320 * cos(24.5 * pi / 180)   # metres, east-west
#> [1] 844.1407

crs(elev, describe = TRUE)$code
#> [1] "4326"
```
:::


30 arc-seconds ≈ 900 m. The raster is in EPSG:4326, the *same* CRS as
`buf_sf` — so we extract with the geographic version, not the UTM one.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
buf_sf$elevation <- terra::extract(elev, vect(buf_sf))[, "elevation"]

summary(buf_sf$elevation)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
#>   148.0   239.0   265.0   260.5   287.0   422.0       1
sum(is.na(buf_sf$elevation))
#> [1] 1
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
boxplot(elevation ~ id, data = st_drop_geometry(buf_sf),
        col = "#1f6f78", border = "grey30",
        xlab = "", ylab = "Elevation (m)",
        main = "Elevation used, by individual")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){fig-align='center' width=576}
:::
:::


Individuals occupy noticeably different elevation bands — a first hint that
they are not interchangeable, and a preview of Class 7.
:::

## Task 6 — Deliberately break it

Do this on purpose, once, so you recognise the symptom for the rest of your
career.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
elev_utm <- project(elev, "EPSG:32736")
```
:::


**First, the good news.** Both objects carry a CRS, so `terra` sorts it out
itself — note the warning it prints:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ok <- terra::extract(elev_utm, vect(buf_sf))
mean(is.na(ok[, 2]))
#> [1] 4.054657e-05
```
:::


**Now the bad news.** Strip the coordinates down to a bare matrix and the CRS
goes with them:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
xy <- st_coordinates(buf_sf)          # just numbers — no CRS attached
bad <- terra::extract(elev_utm, xy)
mean(is.na(bad[, 1]))
#> [1] 1
```
:::


Every value is `NA`. No error, no warning — just a column of missing data that
would quietly propagate into your model.

### Your turn

**6a.** Explain why. **6b.** Find the second way to produce the same failure.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

A matrix has no CRS, so `terra` can only assume the numbers are already in the
raster's coordinate system. It reads longitude 31.8 as **31.8 metres** east of
the UTM 36S origin — a point in the Gulf of Guinea, far outside the extent:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ext(elev_utm)
#> SpatExtent : 337122.45809718, 449698.040805795, 7201293.28983987, 7356754.80881844 (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
apply(xy, 2, range)
#>             X         Y
#> [1,] 31.58639 -25.16421
#> [2,] 32.35671 -23.99802
```
:::


The second route to the same failure is an object whose CRS is *undefined*:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
elev_nocrs <- elev_utm
crs(elev_nocrs) <- ""
worse <- terra::extract(elev_nocrs, vect(buf_sf))
mean(is.na(worse[, 2]))
#> [1] 1
```
:::


Now `terra` has nothing to transform *to*, so it assumes agreement — and fails
the same silent way.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## The habit to build

- **Keep coordinates inside objects that carry a CRS** (`sf`, `SpatVector`).
  Do not pass bare matrices around.
- When `terra` prints `transforming vector data to the CRS of the raster`,
  that is not noise — it is telling you your inputs disagreed. Read it.
- Before every `extract()`, ten seconds of checking:

```r
crs(r, describe = TRUE)$code ; st_crs(pts)$epsg    # same code?
ext(r) ; st_bbox(pts)                              # overlapping numbers?
```
:::

## Task 7 — A map that is not distorted


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
elev_crop <- crop(elev, ext(st_bbox(buf_sf)) + 0.05)

plot(elev_crop, col = hcl.colors(50, "Terrain2"),
     main = "Buffalo tracks over elevation, Kruger NP",
     plg = list(title = "m a.s.l."))

ids <- unique(buf_sf$id)
cols <- hcl.colors(length(ids), "Dark 3")
for (i in seq_along(ids)) {
  d <- buf_sf[buf_sf$id == ids[i], ]
  lines(st_coordinates(d), col = adjustcolor(cols[i], 0.8), lwd = 1)
}
legend("topright", legend = ids, col = cols, lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.75)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why this one is not distorted

`terra::plot()` reads the CRS and, for geographic coordinates, sets the aspect
ratio to `1/cos(latitude)` so that a kilometre east looks like a kilometre
north. Compare with last week's `plot(..., asp = 1)`, which did not.

You can check what it used:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
p <- plot(elev_crop); 1 / cos(mean(c(-25.3, -23.9)) * pi / 180)
#> [1] 1.099824
```
:::

:::

### Your turn

**7a.** Save the buffalo points as a GeoPackage and read them back.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
f <- file.path(tempdir(), "buffalo.gpkg")
st_write(buf_sf, f, delete_dsn = TRUE, quiet = TRUE)

again <- st_read(f, quiet = TRUE)
st_crs(again)$epsg
#> [1] 4326
nrow(again)
#> [1] 24663
```
:::


Use **GeoPackage** (`.gpkg`), not shapefile. Shapefiles truncate column names
to 10 characters, cannot store `POSIXct` properly, are limited to 2 GB, and
are actually 4+ files that people lose track of. GeoPackage is one file, one
standard, no surprises.
:::

## Self-check

::: {.quiz}
`st_crs(x) <- 32736` on an object whose coordinates are longitude/latitude.
What have you done?

- [ ] Reprojected the data to UTM 36S
- [x] Mislabelled the data — the coordinates are unchanged but now claimed to be metres
- [ ] Nothing; `sf` ignores invalid assignments
- [ ] Produced an error

::: {.quiz-feedback}
Assigning a CRS only **writes a label**. The numbers 31.8 and −24.5 are now
interpreted as 31.8 m east and 24.5 m south of the UTM 36S origin — a point in
the Atlantic off West Africa.

It fails silently, which is what makes it dangerous. `st_transform()` is the
function that changes coordinates.
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
Which CRS would you use to compute home-range areas for Leo the vulture, whose
track spans 7°N to 54°N and 108°W to 68°W?

- [ ] EPSG:32613 (UTM zone 13N), where he was tagged
- [ ] EPSG:3857 (Web Mercator)
- [x] An equal-area projection appropriate to the Americas, or per-season UTM zones after segmenting
- [ ] EPSG:4326 — `sf` computes geodesic areas anyway

::: {.quiz-feedback}
A single UTM zone is 6° wide; Leo spans about 40° of longitude, so distortion
far from zone 13 is severe. Web Mercator is conformal and *not* equal-area —
areas at 54°N are inflated by roughly a factor of three relative to the
equator, so it is the worst possible choice for comparing areas.

The right answers are an **equal-area** CRS covering the Americas, or — better
— to **segment first** (Class 6) and estimate separate ranges for the
breeding and wintering areas, each in its own local projection. A single
range for this animal is not a meaningful quantity, whatever CRS you use.

`sf` does compute geodesic areas on 4326, but kernel density estimators need
projected coordinates regardless.
:::
:::

## Before Class 3

- Check `library(move2)`, `library(amt)` and `library(mapview)` all load.
- Try `mapview::mapview(buf_sf)` — an interactive map in one line.
